chapters.title: The Three Rules of Epidemics
chapters.hook: Baltimore's syphilis map changed before the city understood what had moved.
chapters.counterintuition: A sudden outbreak can begin with a tiny shift in who carries it, what clings to memory, or where people meet. Big social change often asks for narrow diagnosis before broad force.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one stalled change and write three headings on a note: carrier, message, setting. Put one concrete fact under each before choosing your next move.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Diagnose fast change by separating carriers, contagious features, and setting; a small shift in one lever can push a whole pattern past threshold.

breakdown.fastRead:
Baltimore saw syphilis rise in the 1990s, and no single cause explained the jump. Crack markets changed where people met. Clinics had less room to treat cases fast. Housing demolition scattered old networks across new blocks. Each fact was small beside the city. Together they changed the map.

+The rule is simple: treat social spread like an epidemic. Ask who carries the agent, what makes it lodge, and where the setting lowers resistance. John Potterat's work on core transmitters shows why average cases mislead. Hush Puppies shows how a fad can leap after the right carriers notice it. The point is not mystery. It is diagnosis before action.
breakdown.deepRead:
Transmission is uneven, so averages hide the path of spread. In a disease outbreak, one person with many contacts can matter more than dozens of isolated cases. In a social fad, one small group can move a style from odd to coveted. The three epidemic levers keep those facts apart: carrier, agent, and setting.

+John Potterat's research on sexually transmitted disease makes the first lever vivid. The task is not to blame one person. It is to see network position. A core transmitter touches enough paths that a slow infection can keep moving. The Gaetan Dugas AIDS tracing story has the same danger. It can tempt people into moral judgment, when the useful lesson is structural: some people sit at intersections.

+Baltimore adds the other two levers. Crack cocaine changed movement and risk. Clinic cuts slowed treatment. Housing demolition moved residents and altered contact patterns. None of those causes had to look huge at first. Their force came from timing and fit.

+Hush Puppies extends the model beyond disease. A quiet shoe can become a signal when the carrier group gives it status and the setting makes that signal visible. The practical move is to resist one-cause stories. First split the outbreak into people, message, and place. Then decide where a small change could do the most work.
breakdown.fullRead:
Hush Puppies looked like a fashion surprise, not a public health case. A shoe that had seemed dated began to appear on the feet of downtown style carriers, and then the signal moved. The lesson is not that shoes behave exactly like bacteria. It is that social spread can cross a threshold after a small change in attention, status, or setting.

+Baltimore gives the harder version of the same logic. Syphilis did not rise because one neat cause arrived. Crack cocaine markets drew people into different patterns of contact. Public clinics lost some power to diagnose and treat quickly. Housing demolition broke up old blocks and sent people into new neighborhoods. The visible outbreak was one curve. Under it sat several moving parts.

+The first lever is the carrier. John Potterat's work on core transmitters shows why a few people can hold a network together. In many epidemics, the average infected person is not the main unit. The critical unit is the person with reach, frequency, and placement. Gaetan Dugas became a famous AIDS tracing figure for this reason, though the useful claim is not blame. Network position can make a carrier look outsized.

+The second lever is the agent. Some messages pass through people with no grip. Others remain in mind long enough to be retold, tried, worn, or acted on. In the opening frame, this is the Stickiness Factor waiting to be named. Reach without retention leaks away. A fad, warning, habit, or health prompt must stay alive after first contact.

+The third lever is context. Behavior bends when the setting changes the cost, cue, stress, or timing around a choice. A city block, a clinic waiting room, a crowded party, or a school hallway can make the same person act in a new way. Context is easy to miss because it looks like background. In an epidemic frame, background can be a cause.

+Good diagnosis keeps the levers separate before joining them again. A clinic delay may matter only because a network has active carriers. A memorable warning may fail if the room gives no cue to act. A visible setting may matter only after a small group gives the behavior status. The frame protects the reader from treating one true detail as the whole story.

+The limit is important. The model does not promise a clever hidden cause for every large shift. It asks for disciplined sorting. Some outbreaks need carrier targeting. Some need a stickier message. Some need a changed setting. Many need more than one. The power comes from testing small, specific levers before spending all effort on broad pressure.

examples.title: Rina's clinic memo

planSpec.domain: city clinic triage during an STI rise
planSpec.audience: health directors diagnosing sudden case growth
planSpec.stakes: a broad campaign could miss the network that is keeping syphilis active
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rina separates core transmitters, clinic delay, and neighborhood movement

examples.scenario: Rina opens the 7:15 a.m. case board in a Baltimore health office and sees syphilis visits clustered near two closed clinics. As deputy director, she has to brief the mayor before the noon budget call. The easy memo blames low awareness. Her second pass marks three columns: core transmitters, treatment delay, and housing moves after demolition.
examples.whatToDo: Rina should frame the memo around the three epidemic levers, then ask for one test in each column before funding a citywide awareness push.
examples.whyItMatters: The Baltimore pattern shows why one broad cause can mislead. Sorting people, agent, and context helps public health action meet the actual path of spread.

examples.title: Desmond tests the shoe signal

planSpec.stakes: money may go into ads before the right carrier group is found
planSpec.requiredBeat: Desmond uses Hush Puppies to look for carriers and context before spend

examples.scenario: Desmond stands at 9:40 p.m. outside a Nolita sample sale with photos of old Hush Puppies on his phone. His footwear startup has cash for one campaign, and the board wants subway ads by Friday. He has to choose between reach and diagnosis. He counts who wears the odd style, where they gather, and which story makes the shoe feel scarce.
examples.whatToDo: Desmond should study the carrier group and the setting before buying ads, using Hush Puppies as a warning that status can move through narrow paths.
examples.whyItMatters: A product can fail with broad reach if the right transmitters never make it visible. The carrier lever can matter before mass attention.

examples.title: Kavita redraws the rumor path

planSpec.audience: communications leads tracing a damaging rumor
planSpec.stakes: a search for blame could miss the network path that keeps the rumor alive
planSpec.requiredBeat: Kavita treats apparent centrality like the Dugas tracing problem

examples.scenario: Kavita sits in a Chicago conference room at 3:05 p.m. with a donor Slack thread projected on the wall. One volunteer appears in every screenshot, so the director wants a public reprimand. Kavita must answer before the board meeting starts. She treats the case like Gaetan Dugas network tracing: central on the map does not mean sole cause.
examples.whatToDo: Kavita should map the rumor's intersections before assigning blame, then address the rooms and handoffs that keep repeating the claim.
examples.whyItMatters: The Dugas example warns against turning network position into moral certainty. The useful question is how the path works.

examples.title: Noor rewrites the reminder

planSpec.stakes: a broad reminder may be noticed once and forgotten before action
planSpec.requiredBeat: Noor treats message persistence as its own lever

examples.scenario: Noor checks a 10:30 a.m. dashboard at the Rutgers student health desk and sees that vaccine emails are opened but appointments stay flat. Her supervisor asks for a larger mailing list by lunch. Noor has to decide before the portal batch closes. She predicts the problem is not reach but stickiness: the note vanishes before students pick a time.
examples.whatToDo: Noor should alter the message so it carries one visible next step, then test whether appointment clicks rise before expanding the list.
examples.whyItMatters: The Stickiness Factor separates contact from action. A message that fails to lodge can touch many people and still leave behavior unchanged.

examples.title: Gideon audits the platform

planSpec.stakes: behavior may be blamed on riders while the setting keeps cueing disorder
planSpec.requiredBeat: Gideon studies context before blaming average riders

examples.scenario: Gideon walks the Queensboro platform at 6:20 p.m. with a clipboard, a radio, and three complaint logs. Riders keep crossing the yellow line near one stairwell. The poster draft blames carelessness, but he must approve it before the print window. He notes crowding, glare, and a broken sign as context cues, not rider traits.
examples.whatToDo: Gideon should fix the platform cues before scolding riders, because the Power of Context asks what the setting is inviting people to do.
examples.whyItMatters: Context can make behavior look like character. A small environmental cue may be the cheapest point of intervention.

examples.title: Marisol separates hallway talk

planSpec.audience: principals responding to fast-moving student talk
planSpec.stakes: punishing the loudest student could leave the rumor's path intact
planSpec.requiredBeat: Marisol separates carrier path from message content

examples.scenario: Marisol hears the first chant at 8:02 a.m. beside the eighth-grade lockers in Fresno. Students say Friday attendance will not count, and three homerooms are already repeating it. As principal, she has to speak before first period ends. Punishing the loudest student is tempting, but she separates the carrier path from the sticky false claim.
examples.whatToDo: Marisol should correct the claim at the hallway junction where it travels fastest, using the carrier route and message wording as separate facts.
examples.whyItMatters: A rumor spreads through both people and content. Treating the loudest voice as the whole cause misses the epidemic structure.

questions.prompt: A city sees a sudden rise in clinic visits after two neighborhood health offices close and several housing blocks are demolished. Which first diagnosis best fits the epidemic frame?
choices: Separate carriers, message features, and setting changes before choosing the intervention.
Fund a general awareness campaign because the clinic rise proves residents need more warnings.
Search for the single resident who appears in the most clinic files and center the response there.
questions.explanation: The epidemic frame starts by sorting the levers. Clinic access and housing movement point to context, while carrier patterns may still matter. A broad campaign or a single culprit skips the diagnosis.

questions.prompt: When a startup notices that its niche shoe is worn by a few downtown stylists, the team wants to buy national ads. What should the Hush Puppies lesson make them check first?
choices: Whether the national ads can mention every feature customers listed in interviews.
Whether the stylists are carriers who make the shoe visible in the right setting.
Whether the company can lower the price enough for large retailers to accept it.
questions.explanation: Hush Puppies points to carrier position and social setting before mass reach. The stylists may create the signal that lets the product tip; price and feature lists do not test that path.

questions.prompt: A donor rumor map shows one volunteer near many message paths. The director wants to blame that volunteer by name. Which response best preserves the Gaetan Dugas lesson?
choices: Ask the volunteer to deny the rumor publicly so donors can see a clear response.
Remove the volunteer from all donor channels while the nonprofit drafts a statement.
Treat centrality as network evidence and inspect the handoffs that make the rumor travel.
questions.explanation: The Dugas story warns that a central node can be mistaken for sole cause or moral blame. Network position tells the team where to inspect transmission, not whom to condemn first.

questions.prompt: Your campus email about flu shots gets opened often, but appointments do not rise. Which change tests the agent lever rather than the carrier or context lever?
choices: Rewrite the email around one appointment action that students can remember after closing it.
Ask resident advisers with many friendships to forward the same email in their halls.
Move the clinic table to the dining hall so students pass it after lunch.
questions.explanation: The agent lever asks whether the message sticks after contact. Resident advisers test carriers, and the dining hall tests context. A clearer appointment action tests retention.

questions.prompt: Which test best reveals whether a transit safety problem is a Power of Context issue?
choices: Compare riders who break the rule with riders who obey it and rank their attitudes.
Change the confusing platform cue for one week and watch whether the same riders behave differently.
Print a stronger warning poster that tells riders the rule has been ignored too often.
questions.explanation: Context is tested by altering the setting around the same behavior. If the platform cue changes conduct, the issue was not just rider attitude or weak warning language.

questions.prompt: A health team keeps asking for the average patient's behavior during an outbreak. What does John Potterat's core transmitter work challenge in that habit?
choices: The team should focus only on medical treatment because network data can distract the clinic.
The team should count public fear because emotion explains why patients avoid treatment.
The team should inspect high-contact positions because average cases can hide the active path.
questions.explanation: Potterat's work makes uneven transmission visible. Averages can blur the few highly connected cases that keep spread alive, so contact position belongs in the diagnosis.

questions.prompt: If a school rumor moves through one hallway, one catchy sentence, and three socially active students, which plan fits the three-lever frame?
choices: Map the students, replace the sentence, and correct the hallway handoff where the rumor travels.
Call an assembly so the principal can warn every grade about repeating unverified claims.
Discipline the three students in private and let teachers decide how to handle hallway talk.
questions.explanation: The three-lever frame separates carrier, agent, and context. The school plan addresses all three without assuming one assembly or private discipline will reach the actual route.

questions.prompt: A colleague says large public shifts must have large public causes. Which Baltimore detail most directly weakens that claim?
choices: The city had more than one expert explanation, so no diagnosis could be useful.
Several small changes in clinics, crack markets, and housing movement combined into one spike.
The syphilis rise was medical, so the lesson should stay inside public health.
questions.explanation: Baltimore weakens proportional thinking. Clinic capacity, drug-market movement, and housing disruption were separate shifts that combined into a sudden public outcome.

questions.prompt: A product team has reach, a memorable slogan, and no setting where customers see one another using the product. What is the missing diagnostic question?
choices: Can the team make the slogan longer so customers receive more reasons to buy?
Can the team survey a broader sample before deciding whether the product has appeal?
Where does the setting make use visible enough for the behavior to spread?
questions.explanation: Reach and message do not settle the context lever. The team needs to find where use becomes visible and socially meaningful enough for spread to build.

reviewCards.front: What are the three epidemic levers?
reviewCards.back: Carrier, agent, and context: who transmits, what sticks, and where the setting makes spread easier or harder.

reviewCards.front: Why does the Baltimore syphilis case resist a one-cause explanation?
reviewCards.back: Crack markets, clinic capacity, and housing demolition changed different parts of the system at once, so the visible spike came from interacting levers.

reviewCards.front: What does John Potterat's core transmitter work add to diagnosis?
reviewCards.back: It shows that spread is uneven. The average participant may matter less than a few highly connected people who keep paths open.

reviewCards.front: What is the useful reading of the Gaetan Dugas tracing story?
reviewCards.back: Network centrality is evidence about transmission paths, not proof of personal blame or a single source.

reviewCards.front: How does Hush Puppies fit the epidemic model?
reviewCards.back: The shoe revival shows that a social signal can tip when the right carriers make it visible in the right places.

reviewCards.front: What mistake does the three-lever frame prevent?
reviewCards.back: It prevents jumping from a large outcome to one large cause. The frame asks which small lever changed before choosing action.

implementationPlan.title: Run A Three Lever Diagnosis
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Before reacting to a fast change, split the pattern into carrier, agent, and context. Name one observable fact for each lever. Then choose the smallest test that would show which lever is doing real work.

ifThenPlans.context: A trend rises faster than expected
ifThenPlans.plan: If the curve jumps, then list the carrier group before debating the message. Ask who touches more paths than an average participant.

ifThenPlans.context: A message reaches people but action stays flat
ifThenPlans.plan: If contact is high and behavior is low, then test stickiness. Rewrite the message around one remembered action.

ifThenPlans.context: People act differently in one place
ifThenPlans.plan: If the same people change behavior by location, then inspect context. Alter one cue in the setting before blaming character.

ifThenPlans.context: The team wants one simple culprit
ifThenPlans.plan: If the room hunts for a single cause, then pause the decision. Require one fact for each epidemic lever.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one active problem at work or home. Write a carrier fact, an agent fact, and a context fact, then run one low-cost test on the weakest column.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review a fast-moving pattern and update the three columns with evidence. Keep only facts you could point to in a scene, log, map, or message.

memorableLines.text: The point is not mystery.
memorableLines.why: The short sentence strips the idea down to diagnosis rather than fascination.

memorableLines.text: Transmission is uneven, so averages hide the path of spread.
memorableLines.why: It names why the Law of the Few changes how a reader looks at data.

memorableLines.text: Context is easy to miss because it looks like background.
memorableLines.why: It makes the setting lever memorable without overexplaining it.

chapters.title: The Law of the Few: Connectors, Mavens, and Salesmen
chapters.hook: Two riders left with the same alarm, but only one woke the countryside.
chapters.counterintuition: Word of mouth is not a fair relay. The same message can stall or race depending on whether it finds people with reach, trusted knowledge, or emotional force.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write the name of one person who bridges groups, one who knows the details, and one who changes the room's mood. Do not put the same name in all three slots.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Match the job to the few: Connectors move messages across groups, Mavens make them credible, and Salesmen turn attention into assent.

breakdown.fastRead:
Paul Revere and William Dawes carried similar warnings on April 18, 1775. The difference was not the sentence they spoke. Revere knew the right towns, the right leaders, and the trust routes that made alarm spread. Dawes rode too, but his warning did not travel with the same force.

+That contrast names the Law of the Few. Connectors bridge many worlds. Mavens collect useful facts and pass them on as help. Salesmen make people feel the force of a choice. A message that needs reach should not be handed to the person who only has charm. A message that needs trust should not be carried by a celebrity with no facts. Influence has jobs.
breakdown.deepRead:
Social distance is not spread evenly across a town, a market, or a company. Some people hold many weak ties. They belong lightly to several worlds, so information can jump from one circle to another. Roger Horchow and Lois Weisberg make that role visible. Their power is not command. It is the number of doors they can open without making the visit feel forced.

+Mavens solve a different problem. Mark Alpert does not matter because he knows everyone. He matters because he gathers prices, features, and practical warnings, then gives them away in a helpful spirit. His advice travels because it feels like service. The receiver does not smell a pitch.

+Salesmen bring the third force. Tom Gau, the Torrance financial planner, shows persuasion as rhythm and rapport. Donald Moine's analysis focuses on mimicry, timing, and emotional alignment. Facts can sit inert until a listener feels safe enough to agree.

+The midnight ride works because it joins message and messenger. Revere had social routes that Dawes did not activate with the same strength. The lesson is exacting: before spending to reach everyone, ask which human function is missing. Need distance crossed? Find a Connector. Need trust in the content? Find a Maven. Need action from the undecided? Find a Salesman.
breakdown.fullRead:
Stanley Milgram's small-world work and the Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon game make one fact hard to ignore: the social world is short because a few people bridge long gaps. Most people know a set of people like themselves. A Connector knows people from many scenes, and that light membership can move news farther than a dense clique can.

+Paul Revere's ride becomes clearer through that lens. The warning about British movement was urgent, but urgency did not spread itself. Revere had standing among colonial groups and a path into local leadership. William Dawes carried a similar alarm, yet the response was weaker. The message was not enough. The messenger's network gave the words reach.

+Roger Horchow and Lois Weisberg show the quieter form of the same gift. They collect relationships across business, art, civic life, politics, and neighborhood worlds. A Connector is not merely popular. Popular people can sit at the center of one circle. A Connector links circles that would otherwise remain apart.

+Mark Alpert gives the Maven role its shape. A Maven watches the market with pleasure. He remembers which stereo is priced fairly, which deal hides a flaw, and which product solves a real problem. The key is motive. Advice from a Maven feels useful because it is offered as a gift, not a trap. That credibility can make a message safe to repeat.

+Tom Gau gives Salesmanship a different texture. The persuasive force comes through warmth, pacing, and small cues that bring the listener into sync. Donald Moine's reading of Gau points to mimicry and emotional timing. This is not mere charm. It is the felt sense that the speaker is with you, so action becomes less cold.

+The hard part is keeping the roles distinct. A famous person may lack bridge ties. A careful Maven may dislike persuading. A natural Salesman may not know enough to be trusted on technical detail. Some rare people overlap, but a campaign fails when it assumes influence is one trait.

+Role confusion is the common failure mode. A team hires a well-known face when it needs a bridge into another community. A manager asks an expert to persuade a frightened room when that expert can only add facts. A founder picks a charming advocate who cannot answer practical buyer doubts. Each error looks like outreach, yet each misses the human channel the message needs.

+The useful test is functional. If the message is trapped inside one group, seek a Connector. If people doubt the content, recruit a Maven. If people understand but hesitate, put a Salesman near the decision. The Law of the Few turns influence from a vague hunt for buzz into a match between social job and human gift.

examples.title: Soren chooses the alarm rider

planSpec.audience: organizers choosing messengers under time pressure
planSpec.stakes: a correct warning may fail if the messenger lacks trust routes
planSpec.requiredBeat: Soren contrasts Revere-style ties with a weaker Dawes-style route

examples.scenario: Soren stands at 5:50 a.m. in a Somerville church basement with a flood map, a phone tree, and fifteen minutes before sirens start. One volunteer has the loudest voice, but another knows the landlords, coaches, and cafe owners. Remembering Paul Revere and William Dawes, Soren has to choose the messenger whose ties will wake the most blocks.
examples.whatToDo: Soren should send the volunteer with Revere-like trust routes, because the warning needs social reach more than volume.
examples.whyItMatters: The same alarm can spread unevenly. A Connector turns a correct message into many trusted handoffs.

examples.title: Helena gives Maven advice

planSpec.audience: retail teams trying to earn customer referrals
planSpec.stakes: paid promotion could sound hollow if buyers need credible detail
planSpec.requiredBeat: Helena uses Mark Alpert's Maven role to make advice useful

examples.scenario: Helena opens the display case at 11:10 a.m. in her Portland audio shop as a customer compares two headphones. The register prompt offers a rebate script, but the customer asks which model fails after a year. Helena must answer before the buyer leaves. She channels Mark Alpert's Maven role and names the cheaper model's real strength and flaw.
examples.whatToDo: Helena should give the precise comparison even when it lowers the sale, making her advice worth repeating.
examples.whyItMatters: A Maven spreads trust by serving the buyer's problem. Useful knowledge travels farther than a polished pitch.

examples.title: Ibrahim coaches rapport

planSpec.stakes: facts may not move a nervous client without emotional alignment
planSpec.requiredBeat: Ibrahim separates Tom Gau-style rapport from more data

examples.scenario: Ibrahim pauses a 2:25 p.m. training video in a Torrance advisory office while a new planner floods a widow with charts. The planner has to call the client back before markets close. Ibrahim points to Tom Gau's Salesman pattern: match pace, lower tension, and let the client feel understood before adding another figure.
examples.whatToDo: Ibrahim should coach the planner to earn emotional alignment first, then use the data only after the client can hear it.
examples.whyItMatters: Salesmanship is not more information. Rapport, timing, and emotional sync can decide whether facts become action.

examples.title: Mei finds the civic bridge

planSpec.stakes: an elegant invitation may stay inside the same donor circle
planSpec.requiredBeat: Mei looks for a Lois Weisberg-style civic bridge

examples.scenario: Mei reviews the 8:00 p.m. guest list in a Chicago museum office and sees the same patrons as last spring. The director wants a prettier invitation by morning. Mei has to decide before the printer locks files. She thinks of Lois Weisberg and searches for a civic bridge who belongs lightly to arts, schools, neighborhood councils, and city hall.
examples.whatToDo: Mei should recruit the cross-domain bridge before redesigning the invitation, because the problem is trapped reach.
examples.whyItMatters: Connectors help messages leave their home circle. A refined appeal can still fail if it never crosses social distance.

examples.title: Lucia repairs the supply list

planSpec.stakes: families may ignore advice that sounds like a school sales pitch
planSpec.requiredBeat: Lucia turns a supply list into Maven-style guidance

examples.scenario: Lucia reads parent emails at 7:35 a.m. in a San Antonio elementary office. Last year's tablet supply list sent families toward costly bundles that broke by winter. Before posting the new list, she adds Maven-style notes: the durable case, the model to avoid, and the store that honors repairs without a fee.
examples.whatToDo: Lucia should publish the guide as practical buyer help, not as a command from school staff.
examples.whyItMatters: Maven credibility grows when advice saves people effort or money. The helper motive makes the message safer to share.

examples.title: Anika splits beta roles

planSpec.stakes: one admired employee may not supply every social function
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anika assigns Connector, Maven, and Salesman jobs separately

examples.scenario: Anika watches a 4:45 p.m. beta dashboard in a Berlin software office while signups stall outside engineering. The CEO wants the most admired designer to promote it alone. Anika has to answer before the launch standup. She assigns a Connector for departments, a Maven for feature proof, and a Salesman for hesitant managers.
examples.whatToDo: Anika should split the rollout jobs across three people, matching each person to reach, credibility, or persuasion.
examples.whyItMatters: Role matching is functional. One admired person may not solve every diffusion problem.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood warning must travel before a storm hits. One volunteer knows every agency head, coach, and shop owner; another has a louder megaphone. Which choice follows the Revere lesson?
choices: Choose the louder volunteer because the storm warning needs to sound urgent.
Choose the bridge volunteer because trusted routes move the warning across groups.
Ask both volunteers to repeat the same script from the same street corner.
questions.explanation: Revere's advantage was network position and trust, not just the warning itself. The bridge volunteer can move the message through many local paths before the storm arrives.

questions.prompt: When a museum invitation keeps reaching the same patrons, which sign would point to a Connector problem?
choices: The invitation copy lists benefits but does not include the museum's newest exhibit.
The donor chair dislikes the invitation color and asks for a more formal design.
The guest list has few people who belong to several civic worlds at once.
questions.explanation: A Connector problem appears when the message cannot jump circles. People who belong lightly to several civic worlds can carry the invitation beyond the usual donor group.

questions.prompt: A parent asks which tablet will survive the school year. The administrator knows one cheaper model has better repairs. What would a Maven-like response do?
choices: Share the repair detail plainly so the parent can make the better purchase.
Repeat the official supply list because parents may distrust extra detail.
Steer the parent to the premium bundle because it makes the school look prepared.
questions.explanation: Mavens gain influence by giving useful, specific information as help. The repair detail solves the parent's problem and builds trust better than official polish.

questions.prompt: Your team has a technical report that people trust but do not act on. Which missing role should you test before rewriting every chart?
choices: A Maven who can add more comparative facts to the report's appendix.
A Salesman who can create emotional assent around the decision.
A Connector who can send the report to a larger mailing list.
questions.explanation: Trust in the report suggests Maven work may already be present. If people understand but hesitate, the Salesman role may convert passive agreement into action.

questions.prompt: Which hiring brief best avoids treating influence as one vague trait?
choices: Find the most charismatic person available and let that person handle all public contact.
Select the person with the largest follower count and ask them to publish each update.
Assign reach, knowledge, and persuasion to people who actually show those separate strengths.
questions.explanation: The Law of the Few distinguishes social functions. Reach, credibility, and persuasion can overlap, but a strong plan checks each role instead of naming one generic influencer.

questions.prompt: A financial planner keeps adding facts while a nervous client grows quieter. What Tom Gau-style adjustment fits the Salesman role?
choices: Slow the pace, mirror the client's concern, and rebuild rapport before adding numbers.
Bring a longer projection so the client sees the technical case in more detail.
Ask a colleague with more contacts to introduce the planner again next week.
questions.explanation: Tom Gau's persuasive force lies in rapport, timing, and emotional alignment. More figures or a bigger network does not address the client's immediate resistance.

questions.prompt: If a campaign has a trusted product expert and a warm speaker but still cannot leave one social circle, which role is most likely missing?
choices: A Maven who can add more details about price, quality, and hidden tradeoffs.
A Salesman who can make the speaker sound more confident during meetings.
A Connector who can bridge the campaign into communities it does not already touch.
questions.explanation: The campaign has credibility and persuasion but lacks cross-group movement. A Connector solves the distance problem by linking otherwise separate circles.

questions.prompt: A manager says Kevin Bacon-style network distance is just trivia. Which practical use best answers that objection?
choices: Use network distance to find bridge people who shorten the path between groups.
Use network distance to rank employees by popularity for every internal message.
Use network distance to replace product quality research with social mapping.
questions.explanation: The practical use is identifying bridge people. Small-world examples make social distance concrete, but they do not reduce all influence to popularity or replace product work.

questions.prompt: A launch team wants one famous employee to handle the beta. Which question would best test whether that employee fits the Law of the Few?
choices: Can the famous employee make the beta feel more exciting in the launch meeting?
Which function does the famous employee actually perform: bridge, expert helper, or persuader?
Will the famous employee agree to send the beta link at least three times?
questions.explanation: The key is function. Fame may help one part of diffusion, but the team needs to know whether the person supplies reach, Maven credibility, or Salesman energy.

reviewCards.front: What does the Law of the Few claim about influence?
reviewCards.back: Influence is uneven. A small number of people can move messages faster because they supply reach, trusted knowledge, or persuasion.

reviewCards.front: Why does Paul Revere outperform William Dawes as a diffusion example?
reviewCards.back: Revere had stronger trust routes and social ties into the right communities, so a similar warning spread with greater force.

reviewCards.front: What is a Connector's distinct job?
reviewCards.back: A Connector bridges social worlds through many weak ties, letting information cross boundaries that would stop a normal message.

reviewCards.front: What makes Mark Alpert a Maven rather than a salesperson?
reviewCards.back: His influence comes from collecting useful market knowledge and sharing it as help, not from closing a sale.

reviewCards.front: What does Tom Gau reveal about Salesmen?
reviewCards.back: Persuasion can come through rhythm, mimicry, timing, and emotional alignment that make the listener ready to act.

reviewCards.front: What failure does role matching prevent?
reviewCards.back: It prevents handing every diffusion problem to one admired person when the message needs a bridge, an expert helper, or a persuader.

implementationPlan.title: Match The Human Channel
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Name the social job before choosing the messenger. Reach, credibility, and persuasion are different needs. The right few are the people whose actual ties, knowledge, or emotional skill match the message's bottleneck.

ifThenPlans.context: The message is trapped in one circle
ifThenPlans.plan: If the same audience keeps hearing the message, then find a Connector. Choose someone with real ties across groups, not just status inside one group.
If listeners suspect a pitch, then use a Maven. Let the most helpful expert share the practical details.
If the facts are accepted but action stalls, then bring in a Salesman. Use rapport and timing to help people cross the decision line.

ifThenPlans.context: One influencer is asked to do every job
ifThenPlans.plan: If one person is assigned the whole campaign, then split the role map. Mark whether that person actually bridges, informs, or persuades.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For one message you need to spread, write the bottleneck as reach, trust, or assent. Ask one person who fits that exact job to help with a small test.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: During the week, track three recommendations you accept. Label the source as Connector, Maven, or Salesman, and note which social job moved you.

memorableLines.text: Influence has jobs.
memorableLines.why: The line turns a vague social trait into a practical sorting rule.

memorableLines.text: Advice from a Maven feels useful because it is offered as a gift, not a trap.
memorableLines.why: It captures why Maven credibility travels without sounding like a pitch.

chapters.title: The Stickiness Factor: Sesame Street, Blue's Clues, and the Educational Virus
chapters.hook: A child can stare at the screen and still miss the lesson hiding in plain sight.
chapters.counterintuition: Attention is only the first gate. A message spreads when its form helps the intended audience notice, remember, rehearse, and use it.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one instruction you repeat often and circle the action verb. Move that verb to the first line, then add one deliberate repeat before the next handoff.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Make the message itself carry the lesson: test attention, remove distraction, repeat the useful step, and give the audience time to respond.

breakdown.fastRead:
Joan Ganz Cooney wanted television to teach preschool children, but reach was not the win. Sesame Street had to hold a child's eye and point that eye toward letters, numbers, and meaning. A funny scene could win attention while the learning target slipped past.

+The Stickiness Factor is the craft of making content lodge. Children's Television Workshop testing treated stickiness as something visible. Blue's Clues pushed the idea further. It slowed the pace, asked direct questions, repeated episodes, and let children feel mastery. Adults may crave novelty. The audience in front of the screen may need a clear path back to the same lesson.
breakdown.deepRead:
Stickiness begins with a hard split: looking is not learning. A child may watch a loud puppet, a moving prop, or a joke and still miss the letter on the screen. Sesame Street became powerful because Joan Ganz Cooney and the Children's Television Workshop treated that split as a design problem. They watched real children, measured attention, and changed the show when the lesson lost the child's eye.

+Blue's Clues made the design rule sharper. Instead of fast variety, it used one host, one animated dog, one puzzle, and repeated clues. The pause after a question was not dead air. It gave the child room to answer. The rerun was not laziness. It gave the child the joy of knowing what came next.

+That lesson travels outside children's television. A safety video, medical instruction, app tutorial, or public notice can reach people and still fail if the key action is buried. The fix is not just more distribution. Put the important bit where the audience looks. Cut the joke that steals attention. Repeat the step that must survive memory. Then test the result with the people who must act, not with the adults who approve the script.
breakdown.fullRead:
Children's Television Workshop began with a bold premise: television could do more than amuse preschool children. It could teach. Joan Ganz Cooney's project joined entertainment craft with research because the medium's reach was not enough. A child could sit in front of the set, laugh at the right moment, and still fail to grasp the educational target.

+That gap makes stickiness practical. Attention is a doorway, not the room. Sesame Street had to learn where children looked, when they drifted, and which production choices helped letters and numbers stay visible. A busy scene might satisfy an adult producer while pulling a child's attention away from the learning cue. Testing made that failure plain.

+Blue's Clues took the insight in a spare direction. The cast was simple. The story moved through one puzzle. The host asked the viewer to help. The pause after each question invited participation. The same episode ran across a week, which would bore many adults. For preschool viewers, the repeat could create mastery. They knew the clue before it arrived. That recognition was part of the learning.

+The deeper point is humility before the audience. Adults are poor judges of what children retain. Experts can love wit, pace, and variety while children need focus, placement, and return. Stickiness is not the producer's feeling that a segment is clever. It is the observed fact that the intended audience can remember and use what the segment was meant to teach.

+The same failure happens in grown-up settings. A hospital handoff video can look polished and leave nurses unsure which sentence to say. A discharge sheet can include every warning and still leave a patient unclear about the evening dose. A factory poster can sit beside the machine while the lockout step hides in the bottom corner. Reach, polish, and approval do not prove stickiness.

+Design has to carry action. Put the clue where the eye already goes. Slow the moment that needs a response. Repeat the exact step that must move from screen to memory. Remove the flourish that wins attention from the wrong object. Test with the people who will use the message under real pressure.

+The limit is that repetition alone is not a cure. Repeating a muddy instruction makes the mud familiar. Pausing after a vague question only lets confusion last longer. Stickiness works when clarity, placement, and rehearsal point toward one usable move. The question is not whether the audience was exposed. The question is what survived exposure.

examples.title: Farah slows the handoff

planSpec.audience: nurse educators simplifying a safety behavior
planSpec.stakes: staff may watch the video without practicing the handoff phrase
planSpec.requiredBeat: Farah borrows Blue's Clues pacing for adult practice

examples.scenario: Farah stands at 6:05 a.m. in a Cleveland simulation lab with a paused handoff video and twelve nurses waiting for shift change. The old clip explains five risks in one rush. She must choose before training starts. Borrowing from Blue's Clues, she slows the key phrase, asks the room to say it, and repeats the exact handoff twice.
examples.whatToDo: Farah should design the handoff around rehearsal, not viewing, so the phrase survives the next noisy shift.
examples.whyItMatters: Blue's Clues used pauses and repetition to create participation. Safety messages need the same path from attention to usable memory.

examples.title: Jamal catches the stolen glance

planSpec.stakes: a funny animation may steal focus from the number relation
planSpec.requiredBeat: Jamal uses Sesame Street testing logic to separate looking from learning

examples.scenario: Jamal watches a 2:15 p.m. screen recording in a Brooklyn edtech office as first graders laugh at a skateboard frog. The lesson is supposed to teach greater-than signs, but eye tracking shows the children miss the numbers. Before the sprint review, he has to admit the app won looking and lost learning, the same split Sesame Street testing exposed.
examples.whatToDo: Jamal should move the animation away from the number relation and retest whether children notice the actual math target.
examples.whyItMatters: Children's Television Workshop treated attention as evidence to inspect. A delightful moment can still steal focus from the lesson.

examples.title: Leonie repeats the dose

planSpec.stakes: patients may hear the instruction once and forget the exact sequence
planSpec.requiredBeat: Leonie treats repetition as a memory tool

examples.scenario: Leonie sits beside a 4:30 p.m. discharge cart in Marseille with a pill bottle, a paper schedule, and a tired patient who nods at every sentence. The old script names side effects first and dosage last. She rewrites it before evening rounds: morning blue pill, dinner white pill, then asks the patient to repeat the sequence back.
examples.whatToDo: Leonie should put the dose sequence first and ask for one repeat, making the key action the part that sticks.
examples.whyItMatters: Repetition is useful when it rehearses the needed behavior. Hearing a fact once is not the same as being ready to act.

examples.title: Bastien watches story hour

planSpec.stakes: adult enthusiasm may hide that children cannot retell the sound pattern
planSpec.requiredBeat: Bastien observes the actual audience before trusting adult taste

examples.scenario: Bastien kneels at 10:00 a.m. beside the carpet in a Lyon library while parents praise the rhyming show. When he asks the children to repeat the sound pattern, most remember the puppet's hat instead. Before next week's program, he audits the scene like a Workshop test and moves the rhyme card beside the puppet's mouth.
examples.whatToDo: Bastien should trust the children's recall test over adult applause, then place the sound cue where their attention already goes.
examples.whyItMatters: Stickiness belongs to the intended audience. Adult delight can hide the fact that children retained the wrong object.

examples.title: Celeste centers the lockout cue

planSpec.stakes: workers may see the poster but miss the action before maintenance
planSpec.requiredBeat: Celeste makes the cue visually central like a tested clue

examples.scenario: Celeste checks the 1:20 p.m. maintenance bay in Toledo and sees a lockout poster half hidden behind spare belts. A supervisor wants a harsher slogan before the audit team arrives. She has to decide before the print order closes. Thinking of Blue's Clues, she makes the lock and tag the visual center, not a footnote.
examples.whatToDo: Celeste should redesign the prompt so the required lockout action sits at eye level beside the machine.
examples.whyItMatters: A message can be present and still miss attention. Placement decides whether the action becomes visible at the needed moment.

examples.title: Hiro reruns the first win

planSpec.stakes: new users may complete a tutorial once without gaining confidence
planSpec.requiredBeat: Hiro uses rerun logic to create mastery

examples.scenario: Hiro reviews a 9:10 a.m. activation chart in a Tokyo product room and sees new users finish the tutorial once, then vanish. The team wants three new features in onboarding. Hiro has to answer before roadmap lock. He predicts a Blue's Clues-style repeat of the first successful task will build confidence better than more novelty.
examples.whatToDo: Hiro should rerun the first core task with a small variation, letting users recognize the pattern and feel control.
examples.whyItMatters: Repetition can build mastery when it returns to the action users must own. Novelty can distract before confidence forms.

questions.prompt: A safety video gets high completion, but nurses cannot repeat the handoff phrase afterward. Which redesign best tests stickiness?
choices: Add a more dramatic opening scene so nurses watch the whole video with more interest.
Send the video to more units so completion data includes a larger staff sample.
Pause on the handoff phrase, ask nurses to say it, and repeat it in the same words.
questions.explanation: Completion shows exposure, not retention. Pausing, saying the phrase, and repeating it test whether the key action moves into usable memory.

questions.prompt: When an app's funny animation draws children's eyes away from the number relation, what did Sesame Street-style testing reveal?
choices: Looking at the screen can hide a failure to learn the intended target.
Animation should be removed from children's lessons whenever math is involved.
Children prefer jokes, so the app should make the number relation less central.
questions.explanation: The testing logic separates attention from learning. The animation may be engaging, but the design fails if it pulls children away from the educational cue.

questions.prompt: A discharge sheet lists every warning, but patients forget the evening dose. Which change fits the Stickiness Factor?
choices: Add more warnings to the sheet so patients see how serious the medicine is.
Place the dose sequence first and ask patients to repeat the sequence once.
Give the sheet to a family member and skip the repeat because the text is complete.
questions.explanation: Stickiness asks what survives into action. Moving the dose and rehearsing it makes the needed behavior easier to remember than a full warning list does.

questions.prompt: Your training team says adults will dislike repeated modules. Which Blue's Clues insight should shape the reply?
choices: Adult preference is a useful signal when the same adults approve the training budget.
Repeated modules work mainly when the topic is meant for preschool viewers.
The audience's mastery matters more than the producer's appetite for novelty.
questions.explanation: Blue's Clues shows that repetition can support prediction and mastery even when adults find it dull. The design should be judged by the intended audience's learning.

questions.prompt: A factory poster is visible near a machine, yet workers miss the lockout step before maintenance. Which test best fits sticky message design?
choices: Move the lockout cue to the worker's eye path and compare behavior for a week.
Ask workers to sign a form saying they saw the poster near the machine.
Replace the poster with a longer policy summary for the maintenance bay.
questions.explanation: Visibility is not the same as attention to the right action. Moving the cue tests whether placement helps the lockout step survive real work pressure.

questions.prompt: A product tutorial shows every feature once, and users leave after finishing it. Which change borrows the useful rerun logic?
choices: Add a survey after the tutorial so users can rank which feature seemed most polished.
Repeat the first core task with a small variation so users recognize and practice it.
Shorten each feature explanation so the tutorial feels faster on the first attempt.
questions.explanation: The rerun logic builds mastery through recognition and rehearsal. A survey or faster tour may improve feedback or pace without helping users own the core task.

questions.prompt: Which claim would be weakest under the Children's Television Workshop approach?
choices: The workshop should watch children because producer taste may misread their attention.
The segment is strong because the adult review panel laughed at the clever scene.
The team should revise if children look at the joke but miss the letter.
questions.explanation: Adult approval does not prove child learning. The Workshop approach gives weight to observed child behavior, especially whether attention lands on the intended learning target.

questions.prompt: If a public message has wide reach but people do not remember what to do, which lever is failing?
choices: The Connector role, because a wider bridge would make the message reach more groups.
The context lever, because people need a different physical place to hear it.
The Stickiness Factor, because contact is not turning into memory or action.
questions.explanation: The problem is not reach. The message is touching people but failing to lodge, so the content's structure, clarity, or rehearsal needs redesign.

questions.prompt: A library story hour delights parents, but children cannot retell the sound pattern. What should the librarian do first?
choices: Observe what children remember and move the sound cue into their attention path.
Keep the story hour unchanged because parent enthusiasm is the audience signal.
Add more puppets so children have several routes into the same reading habit.
questions.explanation: Stickiness belongs to the learner, not the approving adult. The librarian should test child recall and redesign the cue around where children actually look.

reviewCards.front: What does the Stickiness Factor add to reach?
reviewCards.back: It asks whether the message is memorable, repeatable, and usable after contact, not merely whether many people saw it.

reviewCards.front: Why was Sesame Street a design and research problem?
reviewCards.back: Joan Ganz Cooney and the Children's Television Workshop had to learn which production choices held children's attention on the educational target.

reviewCards.front: What is the danger in equating attention with learning?
reviewCards.back: The audience can look at a funny or busy moment while missing the exact idea or action the message was meant to teach.

reviewCards.front: How did Blue's Clues use repetition differently from adult variety television?
reviewCards.back: It repeated episodes, patterns, questions, and clues so children could predict, answer, and feel mastery.

reviewCards.front: What should be tested when a message seems polished but behavior does not change?
reviewCards.back: Test whether the intended audience notices, remembers, and can use the key action under realistic conditions.

reviewCards.front: Why can adult taste mislead message design?
reviewCards.back: Adults may value wit, speed, and novelty while the intended audience needs focus, placement, pause, and repeatable structure.

implementationPlan.title: Make The Message Stick
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Treat the message as a designed object. Identify the exact action or idea that must survive contact. Then test whether the intended audience notices it, remembers it, and can use it without help.

ifThenPlans.context: People saw the message but forgot the action
ifThenPlans.plan: If exposure is high and recall is low, then move the action earlier and repeat it once in the same words.

ifThenPlans.context: A clever element draws attention away
ifThenPlans.plan: If the audience remembers the flourish instead of the lesson, then remove or reposition the flourish. Put the clue beside the target.
If reviewers call the repeat boring, then test mastery with the intended audience before cutting it.

ifThenPlans.context: A tutorial feels complete but users stall
ifThenPlans.plan: If users finish once and do not return, then rerun the core task with a small change. Let recognition build confidence.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one recurring instruction. Test it with one real user or colleague by asking them to repeat the action after thirty seconds.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, collect three places where people saw a message but missed the action. Redesign one for placement, pause, or repetition.

memorableLines.why: It sharply separates seeing from learning.

memorableLines.text: Repeating a muddy instruction makes the mud familiar.
memorableLines.why: It keeps repetition from becoming a lazy cure-all.

memorableLines.text: The rerun was not laziness.
memorableLines.why: It recasts a production choice as a learning mechanism.

chapters.title: The Power of Context (Part One): Bernie Goetz and the Rise and Fall of New York City Crime
chapters.hook: A dirty subway car can change what fear, rule breaking, and restraint feel like.
chapters.counterintuition: Character does not vanish, but the setting can rewrite the script fast. Small cues of disorder, haste, or authority can move ordinary people toward acts they would not predict.
chapters.tryThisNow: Walk through one shared space you manage and name the first visible cue that says rules are weak. Choose one concrete repair you can make this week.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Treat the immediate setting as a behavioral lever: visible disorder, time pressure, and role cues can change what people feel licensed to do.

breakdown.fastRead:
Bernie Goetz became a symbol because the subway already felt like a symbol. In 1984 New York, graffiti, crime, fear, and disorder made one train car feel larger than itself. The same act would read differently after the city changed.

+The Power of Context says behavior is more sensitive to surroundings than we like to admit. Broken Windows treated graffiti and fare-beating as public signals that rules had lost force. David Gunn cleaned trains as an operating priority. William Bratton treated turnstile jumping as a clue about the whole system. The claim is not that paint prevents crime by itself. The claim is that visible cues teach people what kind of place they are in.
breakdown.deepRead:
A place can hand people a script before they know they are reading it. The New York subway in the 1980s gave riders cues of danger and abandonment. That is why Bernie Goetz's shooting became more than a criminal case. It touched the public mood of a city that felt out of control.

+Broken Windows gives the policy form of the idea. Graffiti, vandalism, and fare-beating are small acts, but they speak loudly. They tell riders whether rules are watched. David Gunn's clean-train campaign attacked that signal. William Bratton's fare enforcement did the same from another angle. The point was to change the felt rules of the subway.

+The psychology examples make the claim more unsettling. Philip Zimbardo's prison simulation showed how quickly roles and settings can pull harsh behavior from students. Darley and Batson's seminary study showed that hurry could decide whether people stopped for a groaning man, even after some had prepared a talk on the Good Samaritan.

+Context is not a pardon. Harm still matters. Yet diagnosis gets sharper when the setting is treated as a cause to inspect. Ask what the room, clock, role, and visible disorder are telling people before you decide that character explains everything.
breakdown.fullRead:
Bernie Goetz did not enter public memory only because shots were fired on a train. The story landed inside a New York subway system that many residents already read as unsafe, dirty, and ungoverned. Graffiti covered cars. Fare evasion looked routine. Fear was not an abstract mood. It had a platform, a turnstile, a car, and a daily ride.

+That setting shaped moral interpretation. In the 1980s, Goetz could be seen by many as a vigilante answer to a city that had lost control. Years later, after crime fell and the subway felt different, the same act looked less like rough justice and more like a violent breach. The public did not merely change its mind about one man. The city changed the frame through which the act was read.

+Broken Windows takes that frame seriously. The claim begins with visible disorder. A broken window left unrepaired says nobody is watching. Graffiti on a train says damage is normal. Fare-beating says rules can be crossed in public. These cues need not force anyone to commit a serious crime. Their power is softer and wider: they alter what the place seems to permit.

+David Gunn's graffiti cleanup used that logic. Clean trains were not treated as cosmetic extras. They were treated as signs of control. William Bratton's subway policing of fare evasion worked from a related premise. A turnstile jump was a small offense, but it was also a public lesson about rules. Change the visible lesson, and behavior may shift.

+Philip Zimbardo's prison simulation moves the same idea from subway policy to psychology. Students assigned guard and prisoner roles began to act inside the pressure of the setting. The point is not that personality means nothing. It is that roles, uniforms, rooms, and authority cues can call forth conduct that surprises the person doing it.

+Darley and Batson make the claim almost painfully ordinary. Princeton seminary students walked past a slumped, groaning man on the way to give a talk. The strongest predictor of helping was not their religious reason for being there. It was whether they had been told they were late. Even a Good Samaritan theme did less work than the clock.

+The limit keeps the idea honest. Cleaning graffiti does not mechanically solve every crime problem. Context does not erase responsibility for harm. A rushed person who fails to help still failed to help. But the setting belongs in the explanation. It can make fear feel justified, neglect feel normal, and rule breaking feel cheap.

+The practical question is concrete. What does the place say before anyone speaks? What does the clock demand? What does the role invite? What small sign tells people that care, order, or restraint is expected here? A context diagnosis starts with those cues because people often obey them before they obey their stated values.

examples.title: Nadine watches the turnstile

planSpec.audience: transit managers balancing service and order
planSpec.stakes: ignoring a visible rule break could teach riders that no rule holds
planSpec.requiredBeat: Nadine treats fare-beating as a context signal

examples.scenario: Nadine stands at 7:30 a.m. beside the Eastlake Metro turnstiles with a fare report and two supervisors waiting. Riders hop the gate while a guard stares at his phone. She has to set next month's priorities before the budget meeting. Remembering William Bratton's subway work, she treats fare-beating as a public rule signal, not a tiny loss.
examples.whatToDo: Nadine should reset the visible rule at the turnstile, because open fare-beating teaches riders what the station permits.
examples.whyItMatters: Small violations can act as context cues. Bratton's lesson is that public order signals may shape larger behavior.

examples.title: Oleg cleans the fleet board

planSpec.audience: operations leaders trying to reset norms
planSpec.stakes: drivers may infer that damaged tools and sloppy logs are accepted
planSpec.requiredBeat: Oleg applies David Gunn's clean-train logic to fleet cues

examples.scenario: Oleg arrives at 5:45 a.m. in a Newark delivery depot and sees cracked scanners, coffee-stained route sheets, and a repair board from last month. Drivers joke that nobody checks anything. Before the Monday rollout, he applies David Gunn's clean-train logic: repair the visible cues first so the depot stops teaching neglect.
examples.whatToDo: Oleg should fix the broken tools and stale board before lecturing drivers about discipline.
examples.whyItMatters: Visible disorder can train a norm. Gunn's graffiti cleanup shows why the small sign may carry the larger rule.

examples.title: Sofia lowers the hurry

planSpec.audience: clinical leaders reducing ignored patient distress
planSpec.stakes: rushed staff may miss visible suffering while believing they are caring people
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sofia uses Darley and Batson to reduce hurry pressure

examples.scenario: Sofia hears coughing at 11:55 a.m. near a Boston hospital elevator while residents rush to grand rounds. Two staff step around a patient who has slid low in a chair. She must intervene before the hallway fills again. Darley and Batson are on her mind, so she changes the schedule cue that makes hurry stronger than care.
examples.whatToDo: Sofia should create a staffed pause point before rounds, making the patient check part of the route rather than an interruption.
examples.whyItMatters: The Good Samaritan study shows that haste can overpower identity. Reducing hurry can make caring behavior easier to enact.

examples.title: Kwame adjusts the uniform script

planSpec.stakes: a uniform and title may push staff toward dominance instead of service
planSpec.requiredBeat: Kwame uses Zimbardo's role-pressure warning

examples.scenario: Kwame stops a 3:10 p.m. rehearsal at a stadium gate after new security staff start barking at volunteers. The vests, radios, and raised platform have changed their tone. Before doors open, he has to reset the role. He cites Zimbardo's warning and rewrites the first instruction as guest safety, not guard control.
examples.whatToDo: Kwame should rename the role behavior in training before the uniform and platform define it for the staff.
examples.whyItMatters: Roles can pull conduct from people quickly. Zimbardo's example makes the setting part of ethical training.

examples.title: Rafael frames the subway story

planSpec.stakes: coverage may frame one event as proof of a whole city's character
planSpec.requiredBeat: Rafael situates a crime story in its emotional context

examples.scenario: Rafael edits a 9:25 p.m. crime brief in a Queens newsroom as social feeds compare a platform fight to Bernie Goetz. The headline desk wants a verdict about the city's character. Rafael must file before the late edition. He adds transit-crime data, rider fear, and station conditions so one event is not forced to explain the whole city.
examples.whatToDo: Rafael should place the incident inside its local cues and history before turning it into a symbol.
examples.whyItMatters: Goetz shows how public meaning changes with context. Coverage should reveal the frame rather than hide it.

examples.title: Marta reads the lobby

planSpec.stakes: a neglected lobby may tell visitors that order and respect are weak
planSpec.requiredBeat: Marta treats visible disorder as a norm cue

examples.scenario: Marta enters the Phoenix support lobby at 8:18 a.m. with last week's escalation log. Two chairs are torn, the ticket screen flashes an error, and old forms spill from a tray. Visitors start the day irritated. Before retraining agents, she audits the Broken Windows cues that tell customers the office is already out of order.
examples.whatToDo: Marta should repair the lobby's visible order before asking agents to absorb preventable anger.
examples.whyItMatters: A neglected setting can cue rude behavior before anyone speaks. Context work can remove some friction from the interaction.

questions.prompt: A transit manager sees riders jump a turnstile while staff look away. Which first move best reflects Broken Windows logic?
choices: Treat the visible fare evasion as a rule signal and reset enforcement at that spot.
Ignore the fare evasion until major crimes rise enough to prove a larger pattern.
Post a citywide warning about crime so riders know the system is being monitored.
questions.explanation: Broken Windows logic treats public small violations as cues about whether rules hold. The first move is to change that visible lesson where riders see it.

questions.prompt: A hospital team values compassion, yet rushed residents step around a groaning patient. What does the Good Samaritan study suggest testing?
choices: Whether residents entered medicine for reasons that sound compassionate enough.
Whether posters about compassion should be added near every elevator.
Whether schedule pressure is making hurry stronger than the patient cue.
questions.explanation: Darley and Batson found that hurry predicted helping more than stable identity or talk topic. The hospital should test the time cue, not just values language.

questions.prompt: A delivery depot has damaged scanners and stale route boards. Drivers now treat late logs as normal. Which analogy is closest?
choices: Tom Gau's rapport, because drivers need a more persuasive supervisor.
David Gunn's clean trains, because visible repair can reset what the place permits.
Blue's Clues repeats, because drivers need the same route lesson each day.
questions.explanation: The depot's damaged tools work like disorder cues. Gunn's cleanup treated visible condition as a signal of control, not as cosmetic polish.

questions.prompt: An event security crew becomes harsher after wearing radios and standing on a raised platform. Which diagnosis fits Zimbardo's warning?
choices: The role and setting may be pulling staff toward dominance before they notice it.
The crew needs more legal facts so each guard understands the rules fully.
The platform should stay because visible authority reassures every guest.
questions.explanation: Zimbardo's example points to role pressure and setting cues. Radios, titles, and platforms can shape behavior before staff explain it as personal choice.

questions.prompt: A newsroom wants to make one subway assault proof that the whole city has changed. Which editorial choice best uses the Goetz lesson?
choices: Quote the loudest online reaction because public fear is the story's main evidence.
Delay all coverage until crime trends become simple enough for a short headline.
Show the local fear, crime data, and station conditions that shape how the act is read.
questions.explanation: Goetz became a symbol through the city's emotional and physical setting. Good coverage should make that frame visible instead of turning one incident into total proof.

questions.prompt: A service manager blames rude visitors but the lobby has broken screens, torn chairs, and messy forms. What context test should come before retraining agents?
choices: Repair the visible disorder and track whether escalations fall in the same lobby.
Ask agents to use warmer scripts when visitors arrive already frustrated.
Survey visitors about whether they remember seeing the support rules.
questions.explanation: The broken lobby may be teaching visitors that order and respect are weak. Repairing the visible cue tests context before treating rudeness as fixed character.

questions.prompt: Which claim goes too far beyond the Power of Context?
choices: Graffiti can signal that rules have lost force in a public system.
Time pressure can change whether caring people stop to help.
A cleaned setting removes responsibility from anyone who still causes harm.
questions.explanation: The context claim is diagnostic, not an excuse. Settings shape behavior and deserve attention, but harmful acts still matter and responsibility does not disappear.

questions.prompt: When a city sees petty rule breaking spread in one public space, which question best starts a context audit?
choices: Which offenders have the worst motives compared with the average resident?
What visible cues tell people that rules are weak, ignored, or optional here?
How can the city produce a broader media campaign about civic pride?
questions.explanation: A context audit begins with visible cues and perceived norms. Motives and campaigns may matter later, but the setting's signal is the first object of inspection.

questions.prompt: A supervisor says behavior comes from character, so changing the room is superficial. Which example most directly challenges that view?
choices: Seminary students in a hurry often passed a slumped man despite their stated values.

chapters.title: The Power of Context (Part Two): The Magic Number One Hundred and Fifty
chapters.hook: A group can grow so large that its culture stops knowing its own members.
chapters.counterintuition: Scale is not just more people. Past a rough threshold, trust, shame, praise, and shared memory stop traveling through the same informal channels.
chapters.tryThisNow: List the people in one group you lead or belong to. Mark who knows one another's work well enough to praise, correct, or warn without a meeting.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Protect culture by designing group size; when people stop knowing one another, peer trust and informal discipline need a new container.

breakdown.fastRead:
Robin Dunbar gave a number to a social strain many leaders feel before they can name it. Human beings can track only so many real relationships. Around 150 becomes a rough ceiling for groups that depend on mutual knowledge.

+The Rule of 150 is not a spell. It is a warning about social architecture. Hutterite colonies split to preserve intimacy and discipline. W. L. Gore keeps work units small enough for trust to stay personal. John Wesley's Methodist classes made belief repeatable in known groups. Size is context. If the container grows past what people can know, the culture needs new structure.
breakdown.deepRead:
Group size changes behavior because anonymity changes pressure. In a small community, people know names, habits, favors, debts, and reputations. Praise and correction move fast. Past a certain size, those channels thin out. The group may keep the same values on paper while losing the daily knowledge that made those values enforceable.

+Robin Dunbar's primate work gives the claim a biological spine. Bigger social brains support larger groups, but not without limit. For humans, the rough number around 150 appears again and again in places that rely on stable personal knowledge.

+Hutterite colonies show the cost and discipline of respecting the limit. When a colony grows too large, division is not failure. It protects a way of life that depends on being known. W. L. Gore applies a related idea to work. Small plants and teams reduce the need for heavy command because people can still find, trust, and pressure one another directly.

+The point is not exact arithmetic. A group of 143 can be unhealthy, and a group of 170 can work with the right structure. The useful move is to notice when culture no longer travels person to person. Then split, cell, or redesign the group before asking slogans to do work that mutual knowledge used to do.
breakdown.fullRead:
Robin Dunbar's research begins far from a company org chart. By linking primate neocortex size to social group size, he gave a biological reason to suspect that social life has a carrying capacity. Human beings are not built to hold endless mutual relationships in active memory. Names, histories, favors, status, and obligations take mental room.

+That is why 150 matters as an approximate threshold. The number recurs because many groups need more than membership. They need people to know one another well enough for trust and pressure to work. Below the threshold, a norm can travel through reputation. Above it, the same norm may need bureaucracy, formal reporting, or subgroups.

+Hutterite colonies make the logic visible because they divide when growth threatens cohesion. Splitting can look inefficient from the outside. One community becomes two. Yet the division preserves the dense social knowledge that supports shared discipline. A larger colony might keep the same creed and lose the social setting that made the creed enforceable.

+W. L. Gore and Associates gives the business version. The company behind Gore-Tex has been known for keeping plants and teams small enough that people can know one another. The structure supports initiative because trust has a human scale. Workers can find the right person, judge a promise, and feel peer pressure without waiting for a chain of command.

+John Wesley's Methodist groups show how belief spreads through a small container. The classes and societies made faith regular, social, and accountable. A sermon could inspire, but the small group helped convert inspiration into repeated practice. Rebecca Wells's Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood offers a literary echo. Reading groups made recommendation intimate, not anonymous.

+The mechanism is peer reinforcement. People act differently when they are known. A promise has weight when the group remembers it. A lapse is harder to hide when the people around you know your usual pattern. A good idea gains force when someone trusted brings it into a circle small enough for talk, not broadcast.

+The limit guards against worshiping the number. The Rule of 150 is not a tape measure for every team. Task type, communication tools, history, and leadership all matter. The number is useful because it asks a better question: can this group still carry culture through personal knowledge?

+When the answer is no, the fix may be structural. Split the plant. Create cells. Form classes. Build smaller circles inside the large body. Do not keep adding people to one social field and then wonder why trust feels thin. Culture spreads through containers, and the container has a size.
